intro: To reply to a Google review, open Business Profile, select Read reviews, then select the Reply icon next to the review. Type your reply and select Reply. To change it later, select the Edit icon under your reply, update the text, and select Update. Google checks each reply before it goes live, so it can take a while to appear.

To edit a reply, select the Edit icon under it, change the text, and select Update.
To delete a reply, open the edit view, select the Delete icon, then select Delete.
Google checks each reply first. The check usually takes up to 10 minutes and sometimes up to 30 days.

blocks.text: Reply to a Google review from Business Profile

Start on the web version of Google Business Profile. Sign in with the Google account that manages your listing, then open your profile in Chrome or another browser. Select Read reviews. Each review shows a Reply icon. Select that icon, type your reply, and select Reply. That is the whole flow. Google's help page describes it as Business Profile > Read reviews > Reply icon. The page does not show a last-updated date, so menu names can shift. If a label differs, look for the reply option on the review itself.
Check verification before you reply

Google says you must verify your business before you can reply to reviews. If you do not see a Reply icon, check verification first. Do not assume the page is broken. Google's help text says to verify your business, but it does not name the access level you need. If you did not set up the profile, ask the person who did. They can tell you whether the listing is verified and who has access.

blocks.title: Draft before you paste
blocks.text: Write longer replies in a document first. Read the draft out loud, fix any awkward line, then paste it into the reply box with ⌘ V. You keep a copy for later.
Steps to post a reply, in order

items: Open your Business Profile and confirm you are signed in to the right Google account.
Find the review and select the Reply icon next to it.
Type your reply, or paste the draft with ⌘ V.
Select Reply. Google checks the reply before it goes live.

blocks.text: Edit or delete a Google review reply

A typo or an old phone number is easy to fix. You can change a reply at any time. Google also lets you delete one. Editing keeps the reply in place with new text. Deleting removes your reply from the review. Use delete only when the reply itself is wrong. For a typo or a wrong detail, edit it.

items: Find the review and select the Edit icon under your reply.
Change the text, then select Update to save the new version.
To delete, open the edit view and select the Delete icon.
Select Delete to confirm the removal.

blocks.text: Google checks replies against its content policies before they go live. If Google does not approve the new text, it asks you to edit again. Read the new version against those policies before you select Update. Keep changes short and plain, and remove any line that makes a promise you cannot keep.
What the reviewer sees when you reply

The reviewer gets a notice when you reply. They can still change their review after they read your reply. When they do, the review date updates. So a reply can start a second round. Write for that reader too. Assume the reviewer, a future customer, and a competitor will all read the same words.
Why a reply can take time to go live

Google checks each reply against its content policies before it goes live. Google's help page says the check usually takes up to 10 minutes. Sometimes it takes up to 30 days. If a reply is not approved, Google asks you to edit it. So a missing reply is not always a bug. Look for a note on the review asking for an edit before you post again.
What a good reply looks like

Google's tips page says to avoid identical generic thank-you replies. It says to reply where you can share a useful update or answer a question. It also says to keep replies short and direct. Use the reviewer's name when you have it. A reply that fits under any review tells the reader you did not read this one.

Here is a short reply to a positive review about a late order: 'Thanks, Dana. Glad the team got your order sorted. If anything else comes up, call the shop and ask for me.' It names the reviewer, adds one detail, and gives one next step. That is enough for most reviews.
Replies by type of review

rows: Thank them and name a detail
Their name, the detail they praised, a light invite back
Credit the good, own the gap
One fact you will check, no excuses
Own the problem, move it offline
An apology where it fits, a phone or email for details
A short reply and an offer to talk offline
The facts, no insults, an offer to call
blocks.caption: Choose the goal first, then write the words.

blocks.text: Use the table as a checklist, not a script. Two negative reviews can need different words. The goal stays the same. You want the next reader to see a business that answers clearly and calmly.
Respond to negative Google reviews

Negative reviews need more care. Google advises you to personalize the reply by name. Acknowledge the specific feedback. Apologize where it fits. Then ask the reviewer to move complex issues to phone or email. Google strictly prohibits offering goods or services in exchange for reviews, edits, or removing negative reviews. Keep any offer out of the reply.

Here is a worked example. A reviewer says the soup was cold and the server ignored their table. A good reply names them, apologizes for the cold soup and the wait, says the kitchen will check the timing, and gives a phone number for details. It does not argue about the server or repeat the order. A few sentences is enough.
Mistakes people make with review replies

items: Pasting one thank-you line under every review. Google advises against identical generic replies.
Offering a discount for a higher rating or a removed review. Google strictly prohibits trading goods or services that way.
Repeating a reply across locations without checking names and details.
Assuming a reply is live when it has not appeared yet. Checks can take a while.
Ignoring a request to edit. Google asks you to change a reply that is not approved.
Sharing a customer's order, bill, or contact details in public.

blocks.text: Most of these mistakes come from speed. Slow down for the first sentence. That is where the reader decides whether you care.
Regulated work needs extra care

If you work in law, nursing, accounting, or another regulated field, follow your employer's rules on client or patient data. A public reply should not confirm that a person was a client or patient. Keep the reply general, invite a call or email for details, and check with your compliance lead or practice manager before you post.
Track reviews and replies in Google Sheets

A simple sheet keeps the routine honest. Use one row per review. Add columns for the date, the star rating, the reviewer's name, a short summary, a status, and who wrote the reply. Use status values such as Needs reply, Replied, and Edit requested. Then filter on the status column each weekday. The [Google Sheets for marketers](/for/marketers/google-sheets) page covers shortcuts and limits.

Add a date column for the day you posted. Add another for the day you checked that the reply went live. After a few weeks, those dates show which kinds of review take longest to clear. Use that to plan your time, not to judge yourself.
Draft replies in Google Docs

Google Docs works well for drafts. Keep a page of approved phrases. Include a thank-you that uses the reviewer's name, an apology line, and a line that invites a call. Swap in the details each time. Never copy a whole reply from one review to another. For more routines, see [Google Docs for marketers](/for/marketers/google-docs).
Where Lazur helps, and where it does not

Lazur is a voice assistant for the Mac. Hold ⌥ ⌘ to ask about anything on screen, and Lazur answers out loud. Ask where the Reply icon is, and Lazur draws a circle and a label around it. Ask how to edit a reply, and Lazur guides you one click at a time, waiting for each click.

Lazur does not click the Reply icon, post your reply, or change a review for you. It does not operate other apps. You read the text, decide what to say, and select Reply yourself. That is the honest split. Plans and the free trial are on [pricing](/pricing).

Hold fn to dictate. Dictation writes clean, formatted text at the cursor in any app, so you can speak a draft into the reply box. Lazur can also draft a short reply on request. Treat the draft as a starting point. Fix names, dates, and any promise before you post.
Mac apps for Google review replies

I checked two App Store listings for tools that reply to Google reviews. Review Responder AI says Not verified for macOS. Business Profile for Google lists iPhone and iPad only, and it says it is not affiliated with Google. Neither is verified for Mac use. Google's browser steps are the route it documents, so start there.
Reply with the Business Profile API

Developers can post replies through the Business Profile API. The method accounts.locations.reviews.updateReply creates a reply if none exists and updates it if one does. It only works for a verified location, and it needs the business.manage OAuth scope. That is a build project, not a quick fix. Read the API reference before you plan around it.
What the research says about responding

A 2017 study in Marketing Science looked at hotels, not local shops. Proserpio and Zervas found that responding hotels saw a 0.12-star rise in ratings and about 12% more reviews. After they started responding, they received fewer negative reviews. Those reviews were longer and more detailed.

The same study found hotels tend to start responding after a negative shock to their ratings. They also replied to positive, negative, and neutral reviews at similar rates. The lesson is not to wait for a bad week. Set a routine before the shock arrives.

Treat the study as a signal, not a promise. Hotels are not Google Business Profile listings, so the effect may not carry over to a plumber or a bakery. I found no public study on how long replying takes or what it costs in hours.
Set a weekly reply routine

Pick one fixed time each weekday. Open Read reviews, reply to new items, then check any replies still waiting to go live. Stop there. A short, steady block beats a long catch-up on Friday. Put the block on your calendar and give it a clear name, such as Review replies.
After the routine runs for a week, review the sheet. Look for reviews that sit longest. Those are the ones that need a clearer owner or a template for next time.
Start with the oldest open review

Open the oldest unanswered review first. Write one reply with a name, a detail, and a next step. Post it, then add a row to your sheet. Do the same the next weekday. A few weeks of this routine shows you the rhythm, and the backlog shrinks.

faq.question: How do I reply to a Google review on a Mac?
faq.answer: Use the browser. Open your Business Profile, select Read reviews, select the Reply icon next to the review, type your reply, and select Reply. I found no official Google app for Mac that does this. The two App Store tools I checked do not list Mac support.

faq.question: Can I edit a reply after it is posted?
faq.answer: Yes. Select the Edit icon under your reply, change the text, and select Update. Edits go through the same content check. If Google does not approve the change, it asks you to edit again.

faq.question: How do I delete my reply to a Google review?
faq.answer: Open the edit view by selecting the Edit icon under your reply. Select the Delete icon, then select Delete. This removes your reply. Use it only when the whole reply is wrong, and edit for smaller fixes.

faq.question: Why is my reply not showing?
faq.answer: Google checks each reply before it goes live. The check usually takes up to 10 minutes and sometimes up to 30 days. If the reply is not approved, Google asks you to edit it. Look for that request on the review before you post again.

faq.question: Does the reviewer know I replied?
faq.answer: Yes. The reviewer is notified when you reply. The reviewer can still change their review after reading your reply, and the review date updates when they do.

faq.question: Can I reply without verifying my business?
faq.answer: No. Google says you must verify your business before you can reply to reviews. If the Reply icon is missing, check verification first.

faq.question: Does the FTC rule ban owner replies?
faq.answer: The FTC's final rule from August 2024 bans fake reviews, paid sentiment-based reviews, and review suppression. The FTC press release does not say whether the rule covers owner replies or edits. Keep replies honest, and do not trade perks for changed reviews. Ask a lawyer about your specific case.

faq.question: Can Lazur post the reply for me?
faq.answer: No. Lazur does not click buttons or operate other apps. It can point at the Reply icon, guide you one click at a time, draft text, and take dictation. You read the text and select Reply yourself.

costs.title: Time spent on rework
costs.text: Rushed replies often come back. A reply with a policy problem gets a request to edit. Then you open the review, rewrite the text, and wait for the check again. Google's checks usually take up to 10 minutes and sometimes up to 30 days. Each loop costs time.

costs.title: Ratings that slide before you respond
costs.text: The Proserpio and Zervas study found hotels often started responding after a negative shock to their ratings. Late replies leave the complaint public for longer. Responding hotels in that study did gain about 0.12 stars. That is a modest rise, not a rescue.

costs.title: Trust lost to generic replies
costs.text: Google advises against identical generic thank-you replies. A reply that reads like a template tells readers you skipped the review. Future customers notice that. So does the reviewer, who reads your answer before deciding what to do next.

costs.title: Legal and policy risk from deals
costs.text: The FTC's final rule from August 2024 bans fake reviews, paying for reviews that express a sentiment, and review suppression through baseless legal threats or intimidation. The press release does not say whether the rule covers owner replies or edits. Google also bans offering goods or services for reviews, edits, or removal of negative reviews.

costs.title: A thin profile with few reviews
costs.text: BrightLocal reports that 47% of small businesses have fewer than 20 reviews. The same report says 47% of consumers say that is not enough. The page does not give a sample size, so treat it as a signal. A thin profile makes each reply count more.

causes.title: The listing is not verified
causes.text: Google says you must verify your business before you can reply to reviews. If the Reply icon does not show, verification is the first thing to check. The help page names verification but not the access level you need. Ask whoever set up the profile who has access.

causes.title: Google's content check
causes.text: Google checks replies against its content policies before they go live. If a check fails, Google asks you to edit the reply. It is easy to read that request as a glitch and move on. The request is the fix. Open the review, read the note, and edit the text.

causes.title: Copy-paste replies
causes.text: Copy-paste is the fastest way to reply, and it is the weakest. Google's tips page says to avoid identical generic thank-you replies. Readers spot them fast. They do little for a negative review, and they can read as careless when a complaint is specific.

causes.title: No fixed owner or routine
causes.text: Reviews arrive when nobody is watching. Without a set time to check, they sit. The Proserpio and Zervas study found hotels often started responding after a negative shock, not on a routine. Owners who wait for a bad week tend to reply late and in a hurry.

causes.title: Hard reviews get short answers
causes.text: Negative reviews carry details that need a call. A public reply has room for only a few lines. Owners often reply fast to cool the moment and then say too little. Google advises moving complex issues to phone or email, so the public reply can stay short and clear.

fixes.title: Use the exact path in Business Profile
fixes.text: Open your Business Profile, then select Read reviews. Each review shows a Reply icon. Select it, type your reply, and select Reply. If the icon is missing, check verification before you try anything else. Do not switch browsers to fix a missing icon.

fixes.title: Write three parts, then vary the words
fixes.text: Name the reviewer, add one detail from their review, then add one next step. For example, thank them by name, mention what they said about the staff, and invite them to call the shop if they want to talk. Change the wording each time, so no two replies match.

fixes.title: Move hard cases offline
fixes.text: For a negative review, apologize where it fits. Then ask the reviewer to call or email you for details. Google advises this for complex issues. Keep the public reply short. Do not argue the facts in public, because the reader only sees one side of the story.

fixes.title: Edit a reply when Google asks
fixes.text: If Google asks you to edit a reply, open the review and select the Edit icon under your reply. Change the text, then select Update. Remove the line that seems to break a rule. Keep the reply to the facts, the apology, and the next step.

fixes.title: Draft in a document and read it aloud
fixes.text: Write the reply in Google Docs, read it out loud, then paste it with ⌘ V. Hearing a sentence shows awkward phrasing fast. Check that you did not promise anything you cannot deliver, such as a date or a refund.

fixes.title: Track each review in a sheet
fixes.text: Use one row per review with a status column. Filter for Needs reply each weekday. Mark a row Edit requested when Google asks for a change. The sheet shows what is still open without a search through your inbox.

fixes.title: Fix typos without waiting
fixes.text: A wrong name or an old detail is easy to fix. Select the Edit icon under the reply, change the text, and select Update. Do not leave a wrong detail up while you wait for a better moment to edit it.

fixes.title: Keep offers out of the reply
fixes.text: Do not offer a discount, gift, or free service in a reply. Google discourages offers in replies. It strictly prohibits offering anything in exchange for a review edit or the removal of a negative review. Keep the reply about the experience only.

plan.label: Day 1
plan.title: Check verification
plan.text: Open Business Profile and confirm the Reply icon shows on at least one review. If it does not, check verification before anything else. Start a sheet with one row for each open review and a status column.

plan.label: Day 2
plan.title: Clear the oldest reviews
plan.text: Start with the oldest unanswered review. Use the three-part reply: name, one detail, and one next step. Draft in Google Docs first, read each draft aloud, then paste it with ⌘ V and select Reply.

plan.label: Day 3
plan.title: Handle negative reviews
plan.text: Write a short apology where it fits. Invite the reviewer to call or email for details. Do not argue the facts in public, and do not offer anything in return for a changed review.

plan.label: Day 4
plan.title: Check replies went live
plan.text: Look for replies that are still waiting or that have an edit request. Select the Edit icon under the reply, change the text, and select Update. Mark each row in the sheet as you go.

plan.label: Day 5
plan.title: Set the weekly routine
plan.text: Pick one fixed time each weekday. Add a reminder in Apple Reminders for that time. Filter the sheet on the status column so open items stand out, then repeat the routine next week.
